tier_reason: The repo carries a public harness that times SPARKNaCl.Sign against TweetNaCl's crypto_sign in the same binary with mcycle and checks the signatures match (perf/tsign.adb, perf/tweetnacl.c, perf/perf.gpr, perf/tsign.mk), and the compiler, flags and board are known, but the cycle counts exist only in AdaCore blog posts, a FOSDEM 2022 abstract and a slide deck that are all unreachable here (blog.adacore.com, www.adacore.com and www.slideshare.net return ENOTFOUND; archive.fosdem.org was blocked for the search agent), so the numbers are snippet-only and stay at C per the wave-14 snippet rule.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (two WebSearch result summaries; no page opened): in the February 2021 'Performance analysis and tuning of SPARKNaCl' post, one Ed25519 Sign of a 256-byte message on a HiFive1 Rev B took SPARK 198.03 vs C TweetNaCl 241.83 million cycles at -O0, 98.03 vs 97.65 at -O1 and 93.86 vs 84.99 at -O2 (SPARK slower at -O1 and -O2). After tuning, 'Doubling the Performance of SPARKNaCl (again...)' reports SPARK at 181.74 (-O0), 69.96 (-O1) and 57.82 then 34.94 (-O2) million cycles. A slide deck summary gives final SPARK 24.37 million cycles at -O2 against 84.99 for the original TweetNaCl C and 51.00 for a revised C version, i.e. about 3.5x vs original and about 2.1x vs the revised C (derived from snippet data). The FOSDEM 2022 abstract claims SPARKNaCl outperforms TweetNaCl on Sign by a factor of 3 at all optimization levels. README itself gives no numbers.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GNAT Community 2020/2021 riscv64-elf cross compiler (CE 2019 GCC 8.3.1, CE 2021 GCC 10.3.1 based). perf/perf.gpr applies the same Opt_Switch to both the C TweetNaCl and the Ada code (debug = -g -O0, O1, O2, O3, Os, Og) plus -march=rv32im -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections; the Ada side also gets -gnatp (all run-time checks suppressed). perf/tsign.mk builds with SPARKNACL_RUNTIME_MODE=zfp, RUNTIME_CHECKS=disabled, CONTRACTS=disabled and, as committed, SPARKNACL_BUILD_MODE=debug (-O0); other levels are chosen by editing that variable.
corrections.hardware: SiFive HiFive1 Revision B board (FE310 32-bit RISC-V SoC, code built for rv32im), cycles read from the mcycle CSR
corrections.caveats: Numbers are snippet-only: blog.adacore.com, www.adacore.com and www.slideshare.net returned ENOTFOUND here and archive.fosdem.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED for the search agent, so no cycle table was seen; a verifier with access should read 'Performance analysis and tuning of SPARKNaCl', 'Doubling the Performance of SPARKNaCl (again...)', 'SPARKNaCl with GNAT and SPARK Community 2021' and the FOSDEM 2022 talk. The win is not a language-level codegen effect: both sides run with run-time checks off (-gnatp), and the speedup comes from reworked field arithmetic that the SPARK proofs made safe (Normal_GF limbs bounded to 0..65535, '*' rewritten as a product-scanning multiply on 32-bit limb products U32NL with the carry folded in, fewer carry passes, loop fusion in '+' and '-'), while the C baseline in perf/tweetnacl.c still multiplies i64 limbs (costly on rv32im) followed by two car25519 passes, although it has been given the WireGuard carry and an unrolled inner loop 'as per SPARKNaCl'. The same restructuring could be written in C, so this is a library-versus-library result. Results swing strongly with -O level (SPARK was behind at -O1/-O2 before tuning; README notes the new '*' is slower at -O0). Not an x86 or -O3 measurement; only one embedded 32-bit RISC-V board. README says the latest results are still to be documented.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 139 stars, 14 forks; published in the Alire package index
corrections.why_faster: Not the language's codegen: the Ada build suppresses run-time checks (-gnatp) just like C, so proof-based check removal only reaches parity. The measured gain comes from proof-guided refactoring of the GF(2^255-19) arithmetic (bounded Normal_GF limbs, a 32-bit-product product-scanning multiply, fewer carry passes, loop fusion), which the SPARK range proofs made safe to do; the C TweetNaCl baseline keeps i64 limb products and two carry passes per multiply, which are expensive on a 32-bit RISC-V core.

notes: Keep at C with the asymmetric-algorithm shortcoming: harness, flags and board are public (perf/tsign.adb compares SPARKNaCl.Sign with TweetNaCl crypto_sign in one image and checks SM1 = SM2), but cycle counts are snippet-only and the win comes from rewritten GF arithmetic rather than from SPARK codegen; language_level_claim and same_algorithm corrected to false. A paper-access retier could reach A for the harness if the blog tables are read, still capped by the different-algorithm caveat.

tier_reason: First-party harness is public (src/benchmark.zig, src/cpp_hashtables_wrapper.cpp, C++ flags in build.zig) and BENCHMARKS.md has the quoted numbers, but no CPU model or machine is stated, so not A; tier stays C, and the claim is downgraded because the headline rows are partly harness artifacts and verztable loses most integer-key rows at 3K and 100K elements.

corrections.baseline: absl::flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set, boost::unordered_flat_map/unordered_flat_set and ankerl::unordered_dense::map/set (src/cpp_hashtables_wrapper.cpp); integer keys use each library's default hash, string keys use std::string_view with a shared wyhash. The 'std' column is Zig's std.AutoHashMap/StringHashMap, not std::unordered_map.
corrections.workload: u32, u64 and random-length (8-64 char) string keys with void, 4-byte and 64-byte values, at 100, 3K and 100K elements (1M appears only in the memory table); 16 operation mixes (random and sequential insert, reserved insert, update, random lookup, high load, lookup miss, tombstone, delete, iteration, churn, mixed, read-heavy, write-heavy, update-heavy, zipfian); ns per operation, 15 iterations; C++ tables called from Zig through per-operation extern "C" wrappers.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'outperforms Google's Abseil, Boost, and Ankerl on mixed workloads'. BENCHMARKS.md, 100-element u32 set: Reserved Ins. 5 ns vs Abseil 13 / Boost 14 / Ankerl 9 (but the C++ tables are never reserved, see caveats); Delete 4 vs 13 / 6 / 6; Lookup Miss 1 vs 5 / 2 / 3; Tombstone 5 vs 16 / 6 / 8; losses in the same table: Rand. Lookup 3 vs Boost 2, Write-Heavy 12 vs Ankerl 8. Across all 432 per-configuration rows verztable beats the best of the three C++ tables in 156, ties 37 and loses 239; geometric-mean time ratio C++/verztable is about 1.03 vs Boost, 1.33 vs Abseil and 1.46 vs Ankerl (derived from page data). At 100K integer keys it loses nearly every row to Abseil and Boost (u32 set: 0 wins of 16; geomean 0.61x of Boost's speed); its clearest wins are on string keys (8-10 of 16 rows per configuration) and on 100-element tables. The page's 27-configuration average table shows verztable ahead on 10 of 16 operations and behind on random/sequential insert, lookup miss, iteration and write-heavy.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2+ with -O ReleaseFast for verztable and the Zig std maps; the C++ wrapper and Abseil sources are compiled by Zig's bundled clang with -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti (build.zig); native target by default; no LTO configured, so C++ calls are not inlined into the Zig benchmark loop.
corrections.caveats: Own harness, no CPU model or OS stated. Harness asymmetries: (1) 'Reserved Ins.' calls ensureTotalCapacity for verztable and Zig std, but benchCpp's setup for .insert_reserved does nothing and the wrapper has no reserve function, so the C++ columns in that row are plain un-reserved inserts (verztable 'wins' 22 of 27 such rows); (2) every C++ operation goes through a non-inlined extern "C" call (insert also memcpys the value into a temporary), which adds roughly a call's cost to 1-5 ns operations, the size range where verztable wins most; the README's argument that Ankerl's 0 ns iteration shows minimal FFI overhead does not hold because iteration is a single wrapper call that counts inside C++. The string fast path (keys up to 8 bytes packed into a u64) and stored 64-bit hashes are design features the competitors do not use. Uses about 25% more memory than the competitors by the README's own trade-off note (string sets 3.3 MB vs 1.9-2.0 MB at 100K). Verstable (C) is the algorithmic inspiration, not a benchmark target. 15 stars, single author.
corrections.why_faster: Algorithmic, not Zig codegen: Verstable-style open addressing with 16-bit metadata per bucket (4-bit hash fragment filters most non-matching keys without touching bucket data), tombstone-free deletion, a packed fast path for string keys of 8 bytes or fewer and stored full 64-bit hashes that skip memcmp. Part of the measured margin on small tables comes from the harness (inlined Zig calls versus per-operation FFI calls into C++, and the un-reserved C++ 'Reserved Ins.' row).

notes: Real table with a public harness, but the claim is overstated: the cited Reserved Ins. win compares reserved verztable against un-reserved C++ tables, all C++ operations pay a non-inlined FFI call, and verztable loses 239 of 432 rows to the best C++ table (beats Boost by only about 3% geomean, loses most integer rows at 3K/100K). Record shortcomings: harness asymmetry (no reserve for C++, per-op FFI), no CPU model, not faster than Boost on integer keys at scale, higher memory use.

tier_reason: The kostya/benchmarks README (UPDATE 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G, Zig 0.16.0, gcc 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8) shows Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s, with code (base64/test.zig, base64/test-nolib.c) and flags (common/commands.mk, base64/Makefile) public, so the harness is A-grade; capped at C because it is not like for like: Zig calls std.base64, which decodes 16 characters per step through four pre-shifted lookup tables with one validity check and a 16-byte store and encodes 12 bytes per u128 load, while the C program is a hand-written per-character decoder with a branch per character and newline skipping (same asymmetric-kernel cap as the kostya matmul D entry in batch-02).

corrections.claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks base64 table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README updated 2026-07-19): Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s, about 1.31x and 1.59x faster (derived from page data); Rust 0.842 s also beats both. The same table has C/clang (aklomp) 0.095 s and C/gcc (aklomp) 0.097 s, about 7.4x faster than Zig, and PHP 0.065 s (its C base64) fastest overall; C++ with libcrypto takes 3.664 s.
corrections.caveats: Not the same algorithm: Zig uses std.base64 (checked in lib/std/base64.zig at the 0.15.2 tag and master on the GitHub mirror; the 0.16.0 tag is not on GitHub), whose decoder ORs four 256-entry u32 tables pre-shifted per character position, checks validity once per 4 characters and writes 16 bytes per u128 store, and whose encoder reads 16 bytes as a u128 and emits 16 characters per 12 input bytes; base64/test-nolib.c uses one decode table, branches on every character, scans for \n and \r before each quantum (MIME tolerance Zig's standard decoder does not provide) and stores byte by byte. So the win is a library implementation difference; the SIMD C library (aklomp) is about 7x faster than Zig, and the same four-table technique is available in C (e.g. Chromium modp_b64). Buffers: Zig uses a FixedBufferAllocator and C uses stack VLAs, so 'newly allocated buffers' cost nothing on either side; the Zig input is a comptime constant ("a" ** 131072) and the C input a memset stack array. Zig is built with zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (native CPU by default), C with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto. Medians with MAD from one machine; the README states no flags in prose (they are in common/commands.mk).
corrections.why_faster: Library implementation, not Zig codegen: Zig's std.base64 decoder uses four pre-shifted lookup tables (one OR per character, one validity test per quantum, 16-byte stores) and its encoder processes 12 input bytes per u128 load, while the C baseline is a simpler per-character scalar loop with per-character error branches and newline skipping.

notes: Numbers verified on the README; harness is reproducible (code, flags, CPU, versions) but the win comes from Zig's std.base64 algorithm against a naive hand-written C loop, so it stays C with same_algorithm false; the best C (aklomp/base64, SIMD) is about 7x faster than Zig. Record shortcoming: different algorithm on each side, not a language effect.
